summary: This document extends ABNF, the notation for writing protocol syntax, with a way to specify US-ASCII string literals that are matched case-sensitively. Base ABNF string matching is case-insensitive.

eli5.summary: Normally, in these rules, capital and small letters count as the same. This RFC adds a way to say capital and small letters must match exactly.

questions: how to make abnf strings case sensitive
subtitle: A %s prefix that lets ABNF grammars say a quoted string must match letter case exactly.

tldr.problem: ABNF string literals always match without regard to letter case, so writing a case-sensitive rule meant spelling out each character by its number, which is inconvenient and error prone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two prefixes for quoted strings: %s for case-sensitive matching and %i for case-insensitive matching. A string with no prefix stays case-insensitive.
tldr.outcome: Grammars can now write case-sensitive literals directly. The RFC updates RFC 5234 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 7405 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5234. The unit metadata shows no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why ABNF Needed a Change
sections.content:
ABNF (Augmented Backus-Naur Form) is a notation for writing down protocol syntax. In the base definition, RFC 5234, quoted US-ASCII string literals are matched without regard to letter case.

That is often what you want. When it is not, the old workaround was to write the characters by their numeric values, which the RFC calls inconvenient and error prone to write and read. RFC 7405 is written as a set of changes to RFC 5234.
sections.eli5: The old rule book treated big and small letters as the same. If you wanted them to be different, you had to write every letter as a secret number code, which was a pain.

sections.title: The %s and %i Prefixes
sections.content:
A literal text string is written in quotation marks and may now carry a prefix. %s means case-sensitive and %i means case-insensitive. With no prefix, the string is case-insensitive, exactly as before, so it is the same as writing %i. This keeps older grammars working.

Both rulename = %i"aBc" and rulename = "abc" match "abc", "Abc", "aBc" and every other capitalization. In contrast, rulename = %s"aBc" matches only "aBc".
sections.eli5: Put a little %s in front and the letters must match exactly, big or small. Leave it off and big and small letters count as the same.

sections.title: What Changes in RFC 5234
sections.content:
The RFC makes two replacements in RFC 5234. It replaces the last half of Section 2.3, starting at "ABNF permits the specification of literal text strings", and it replaces the char-val rule in Section 4.

The new char-val is either a case-insensitive-string (an optional %i and a quoted string) or a case-sensitive-string (%s and a quoted string). The old numeric style, such as %d97 %d98 %d99 or %x61.62.63, still works and matches only the lowercase text abc, but a prefixed string has a clear readability advantage.

The Security Considerations section says only that security is truly believed to be irrelevant to this document.
sections.eli5: Two spots in the old rule book get new pages. Everything people wrote before still works.

data.title: ABNF definition of char-val
data.code:
char-val       =  case-insensitive-string /
                  case-sensitive-string

case-insensitive-string =
                  [ "%i" ] quoted-string

case-sensitive-string =
                  "%s" quoted-string

quoted-string  =  DQUOTE *(%x20-21 / %x23-7E) DQUOTE
                       ; quoted string of SP and VCHAR
                       ;  without DQUOTE

references.text: Crocker, D. and P. Overell, "Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF", STD 68, RFC 5234, January 2008.
